edges.description: The granulomatous lesion is the tuberculous salpingitis itself, usually bilateral.
The lesion is seen histologically as caseating epithelioid granulomas.
Chronic granulomatous inflammation destroys the endosalpinx and leads to beading, closure of the tubes and hydrosalpinx.
The inflamed tubes form pyosalpinx and tubo-ovarian masses and become bound down by dense adhesions.
Infection spreads from the tubes to the endometrium, which is involved in more than half of cases.
Scarring and destruction of the tubal wall close the lumen.
Closure of the tube traps clear fluid as a hydrosalpinx.
Blocked and damaged tubes cause tubal-factor infertility.
A damaged endosalpinx favours implantation in the tube.
Caseous material fills the tube as a pyosalpinx and can form a tubo-ovarian abscess.
Peritubal and periovarian inflammation leaves pelvic adhesions.
Spread to the upper peritoneum gives perihepatic (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis) adhesions.
Extension to the ovary gives tuberculous oophoritis in a minority of women.
Adnexal masses and pelvic adhesions cause chronic pelvic pain.
The endometrial lesion is tuberculous endometritis.
Endometrial destruction leaves intrauterine adhesions.
Endometrial destruction with adhesions causes secondary amenorrhoea.
Endometrial damage reduces menstrual flow and frequency.
Active endometrial inflammation can cause heavy menstrual bleeding.
Endometrial damage impairs implantation and lowers pregnancy rates, even with in-vitro fertilization.
Reduced immunity makes spread of bacilli from the primary focus to the genital tract more likely; the cited sources do not identify the intervening steps.
